## Intent

The finding admits it is already in the public record: a prior audit, a documented design decision, a known issue. Submitting it signals that the prior audit was not read, which is worse than not submitting.

## Detection signals

Signals are admission phrases: "previously reported", "already known", "known issue", "documented as intended", or a named prior audit that covered or accepted the surface. A bare mention of "prior audit" is deliberately NOT a signal, because "the prior audit missed this" is the opposite claim. The rule fires on the report's own words, which is why it cannot find the *real* duplicate that the report does not mention.

Patterns are case-insensitive regular expressions matched against the full text of the
draft finding, subject to the engine rules below.

**Fires when at least one of these matches:**

```text
  previously (reported|identified|reviewed|raised|accepted|assessed)
  already (reported|known|acknowledged|accepted|covered|raised)
  known (issue|limitation|characteristic|design)
  (prior|earlier|previous) audit .{0,40}(covered|identified|accepted|reported|raised)
  documented (as |)(intended|design)
```

## Escape hatches

Six suppression patterns, all negations: "no prior audit", "not covered by a prior review", "no known", "not previously", "new since", "first audit of". A negated statement is the opposite signal — it says the surface is new — and without these the rule fired on exactly the findings it should have passed.

**Suppressed when any of these matches anywhere in the finding:**

```text
  no prior audit
  not (covered|found|identified) (by|in) (a |any )?prior
  no (known|previously)
  not previously
  new since
  first (audit|review) of
  (prior|earlier|previous) audit .{0,40}(missed|did not cover|does not cover|never covered)
```

## Known false-positive modes

These are the shapes where the rule fires on something it should not. They are the
reason a firing is a prompt to check, not a verdict.

- A report that cites a prior audit to distinguish its own finding from it, where the distinguishing language is not one of the six negations.
- A finding about a *regression* that reintroduces a previously fixed issue.
- A report that quotes the program's known-issues list in order to argue the entry does not cover this case.

## Synthetic examples

Both examples are synthetic. They describe no real report and no real target.

**Fires:** "This was already reported in a prior audit and accepted as intended."

**Does not fire:** "No prior audit covers this module; the surface is new since the last review."

## Corrective action

Do not submit. Prior audit findings are part of the public record; submitting a known design characteristic signals you did not read the prior audit.

## Changelog

| Date | Change |
|---|---|
| 2026-10-08 | Escape hatches for negated forms added before the first catalog commit. The rule previously over-fired on findings whose whole point was that the surface was new. |
| 2026-10-10 | A bare "prior audit" removed as a signal. "The prior audit missed this" is the opposite claim and the old rule hard-killed it; the engine's negation window now applies on top of the explicit escape hatches. |
